synonyms: It's a bit early for us
Come back when you have more data
We usually come in a little later
We'd like to see more progress first
en.h1: “You’re too early for us” — what it might mean and how to reply
en.shortAnswer: Usually a stage or evidence gap, sometimes a polite pass. The difference shows up in whether the investor names a specific milestone and invites an update — so ask for that milestone, keep raising from earlier-stage investors, and come back only with real progress.

interpretations.possibility: Stage or cheque-size mismatch: the fund typically invests later, or writes cheques too large for your round.
interpretations.contextualClues: Their recent deals are mostly later-stage; they mention minimum revenue, round size or ownership targets; the feedback is about how the fund works rather than about your company.

interpretations.possibility: A specific risk they want retired first — customer demand, retention, a technical proof point or a key hire.
interpretations.contextualClues: They name a metric or milestone, ask detailed questions about that area, or ask you to send an update when you reach it.

interpretations.possibility: A polite decline with no real plan to reconsider.
interpretations.contextualClues: No milestone, no timeframe and no request for updates; a one-line reply after a long silence; the fund does invest at your stage but offers no specifics.

positiveSignals: They name a concrete milestone (e.g. a revenue level, number of paying customers, retention cohort).
They ask you to send an update at a specific point.
They introduce you to an earlier-stage investor or offer feedback on the deck.
The person who said it is a decision-maker who spent real time on your business.
weakSignals: No milestone, no timeframe and no request to stay in touch.
It arrives as a short reply after weeks of silence.
The fund has recently invested at your stage, which suggests the issue may be conviction rather than stage.
The wording reads like a template sent to many founders.
en.clarifyingQuestion: Thanks for the candid feedback. So I can focus on the right things — is there one specific milestone (customers, retention or something else) that would make it worth revisiting?
en.recommendedAction: Log the feedback and any milestone they mention. Check the fund's typical stage before drawing conclusions. Keep the round moving with pre-seed/seed specialists now, and re-contact this investor only when you have material progress against the milestone they named.
en.followUpTimingNote: Reply once within one or two business days to thank them and ask the clarifying question. After that, reconnect when you hit the milestone — not on a calendar reminder alone.
en.editableReplyTemplate:
Hi [Investor name],

Thank you for taking the time to look at [Company] and for the candid feedback.

So I focus on the right things: is there one specific proof point — for example [metric, e.g. paying customers or retention] — that would make a future conversation worthwhile? If so, I'd be glad to send a short update once we've reached it.

And if you know an investor who typically backs companies at our stage, I'd really appreciate an introduction.

Best,
[Your name]

exampleScenario.description: Hypothetical: a seed-stage B2B software founder with three paying pilots pitches a fund whose recent deals are mostly Series A. The partner says “you’re too early for us” and mentions they usually want a longer revenue history. The stage-mismatch reading is the most plausible here. The founder thanks them, asks whether an update after two more quarters of revenue would be useful, and refocuses the round on seed specialists.

en.phrase: It's not the right fit for us.
synonyms: It doesn't fit our thesis
This is outside our focus
We don't invest in this space
Not a fit for our fund
en.h1: “It’s not the right fit for us” — what it might mean and how to reply
en.shortAnswer: Most often a clear no tied to the fund's mandate — sector, stage, geography or cheque size — and occasionally a polite way to express doubts about the market. Either way, it is rarely worth arguing. Ask once which dimension didn't fit, ask for a referral if the conversation was warm, and move on.

interpretations.possibility: A genuine mandate mismatch: sector, stage, geography, cheque size or ownership target sits outside what the fund can do.
interpretations.contextualClues: They name the constraint; their portfolio and website confirm it; the decline comes quickly, sometimes before a meeting.

interpretations.possibility: A conviction gap expressed politely — they don't believe in the market size, the approach or the timing.
interpretations.contextualClues: They invest in adjacent companies at your stage; the meeting included sceptical questions about the market; no specific constraint is named.

interpretations.possibility: A portfolio conflict — they already back a company that overlaps with yours.
interpretations.contextualClues: A similar company appears in their portfolio; the reasoning is vague; they decline after learning more about your positioning.

positiveSignals: They explain precisely which part of the mandate doesn't fit — useful for targeting.
They suggest a better-fit fund or offer an introduction.
They say what would need to change for a future conversation (rare, but useful).
weakSignals: A generic template email with no reason.
No reply to a polite request for the reason — treat that as final.
They emphasise how busy they are rather than anything about your company.
en.clarifyingQuestion: Thanks for the clear answer — it genuinely helps. Was it mainly stage, sector or geography? It will help me focus on better-fit investors.
en.recommendedAction: Ask the clarifying question once, then move this investor out of your active pipeline. Use what you learn to tighten your target list (stage, sector, geography, cheque size). If the relationship was warm, ask for one referral.
en.followUpTimingNote: Reply once within a couple of business days. Don't follow up again this round; revisit only if their thesis or your company changes materially.
en.editableReplyTemplate:
Hi [Investor name],

Thanks for the clear answer — I appreciate you not leaving us guessing.

If you have a moment, was it mainly a question of stage, sector or geography? It will help me focus on better-fit investors.

And if a fund comes to mind that typically backs [short description of Company] at our stage, I'd be grateful for a pointer.

All the best,
[Your name]

exampleScenario.description: Hypothetical: a hardware-plus-software startup pitches a fund that only invests in pure software. The associate replies “not the right fit for us” the same day. The mandate-mismatch reading is most plausible. The founder replies once asking whether hardware was the issue, gets a one-line confirmation, and removes hardware-averse funds from the target list.

synonyms: Keep us posted
Let's stay in touch
Keep me updated on your progress
Add me to your investor updates
en.h1: “Let’s keep in touch” — what it might mean and how to reply
en.shortAnswer: An open door, not a commitment. It can mean genuine long-term interest, interest that is waiting for a specific signal, or a gentle no. A precise request for a particular update is a stronger signal than a warm but generic sign-off.

interpretations.possibility: Interested, but waiting for a signal — a milestone, a lead investor or momentum in your round.
interpretations.contextualClues: They say what they'd like to see, ask when you expect to close, or ask who else is involved.

interpretations.possibility: Genuine long-term relationship interest without a current decision.
interpretations.contextualClues: They ask to be added to your investor updates, reply to them, or offer help unrelated to investing.

interpretations.possibility: A polite soft no that keeps the relationship pleasant.
interpretations.contextualClues: No specific request, no question about timing, and the phrase ends the conversation rather than opening a next step.

positiveSignals: They ask for a specific update (a metric, a launch, a hire).
They propose a check-in at a defined point.
They reply to or comment on your updates.
They make an introduction without being asked.
weakSignals: Generic warmth with no question about your business.
No acknowledgement of later updates.
It follows a meeting where they did most of the talking about the fund rather than asking about you.
en.clarifyingQuestion: Happy to. What development would be most useful for me to share — and would an update after [milestone] be helpful?
en.recommendedAction: Treat them as outside your active round unless they say otherwise. With their agreement, add them to a concise investor update and share material progress. Don't send weekly check-ins; send high-signal updates.
en.followUpTimingNote: Send one short reply now. Afterwards, update when something material happens — a monthly or quarterly cadence is a common upper bound for unsolicited updates.
en.editableReplyTemplate:
Hi [Investor name],

Thanks again for the conversation — happy to stay in touch.

So my updates are actually useful to you: what would be most relevant to hear about — [option A, e.g. revenue growth], [option B, e.g. key hires], or something else? I'm planning to share a short update after [milestone].

Would it be OK to add you to our investor update list? It goes out roughly [frequency] and is easy to unsubscribe from.

Best,
[Your name]

The founder confirms the launch month, adds the angel to the quarterly update with permission, and sends the update with launch results.

synonyms: Let's reconnect in a few months
Ping us next quarter
Timing isn't right for us now
Reach out again after the summer
en.h1: “Circle back next quarter” — what it might mean and how to reply
en.shortAnswer: A timing message that can be real (fund pacing, partner bandwidth, their own fundraising) or a soft pass that uses time as the reason. What separates them is whether the investor says what would be different next quarter and agrees to a date.

interpretations.possibility: They want to see progress over the interval — the delay is a way to get more data.
interpretations.contextualClues: They mention a metric, product release or hire they'd like to see by then.

interpretations.possibility: A genuine timing constraint on their side: deployment pacing, partner bandwidth, or raising their own fund.
interpretations.contextualClues: They explain the constraint openly; they suggest a month or put a call in the calendar.

interpretations.possibility: A soft pass that avoids saying no.
interpretations.contextualClues: No reason, no metric, no date; the phrase comes after limited engagement in the meeting.

positiveSignals: They name what they want to see next quarter.
They propose or accept a specific date.
They explain a concrete internal reason for the timing.
weakSignals: No reason or metric given.
They decline to put anything in the calendar.
Your round will likely close before then — and they know it.
en.clarifyingQuestion: Happy to reconnect then. What would you most want to see by next quarter — and is there a particular month that works best?
en.recommendedAction: Set one dated reminder and note what they asked to see. Don't pause your round waiting for them. If your timeline means you'll close earlier, say so politely so they can decide.
en.followUpTimingNote: Reconnect around the month they named with a short update. If there's no reply, one gentle nudge a week or two later, then let it go.
en.editableReplyTemplate:
Hi [Investor name],

Thanks — happy to reconnect next quarter.

So the next conversation is useful: what would you most like to see by then? I'd expect to have [progress you expect, e.g. results from our first enterprise pilot].

For transparency, we're currently aiming to close our round by [target month]. If that changes the picture for you, I'm glad to share more before then.

Best,
[Your name]

The genuine-timing reading is plausible, but the founder's round closes in six weeks. The founder replies with the close date and keeps the round moving; the partner chooses to pass this round but asks to be on future updates.

synonyms: Can you send over your deck?

en.h1: “Send me your deck” — what it might mean and how to reply
en.shortAnswer: Neutral on its own. It is usually an initial screening step and sometimes a sign of real early interest; what matters is what it follows and what happens after. Send a concise, current deck promptly and propose a specific next step.

interpretations.possibility: Initial screening — a low-cost way for the fund to filter many companies.
interpretations.contextualClues: Asked at an event or by email without a conversation; often by an analyst or associate; no next step mentioned.

interpretations.possibility: Genuine preliminary interest after a good conversation.
interpretations.contextualClues: It follows specific questions about your business; they mention who else will review it or suggest a call after reading.

interpretations.possibility: A polite way to end a conversation — or market mapping for a thesis the fund is exploring.
interpretations.contextualClues: Very broad interest in your sector rather than your company; no follow-up questions after you send it.

positiveSignals: They ask specific follow-up questions after reading.
They propose a call or name the next reviewer.
They request additional material (data room, model, references).
weakSignals: No acknowledgement after you send it.
The request came with no context about your company specifically.
They ask for highly sensitive data before any conversation.
en.clarifyingQuestion: Of course — I'll send it today. After you've had a look, would a 20-minute call to go through questions make sense?
en.recommendedAction: Send a concise, up-to-date deck within a day, with a three-to-four-line summary in the email body and a proposed next step. Share only what you are comfortable sharing at this stage.
en.followUpTimingNote: Send within 24–48 hours. If there's no reply, one short follow-up after about a week, ideally with a small, real update.
en.editableReplyTemplate:
Hi [Investor name],

Thanks for your interest in [Company] — the deck is attached.

In short: we help [customer] [outcome]. Since [timeframe] we've [key progress], and we're raising [round size/stage] to [main use of funds].

After you've had a look, would a 20-minute call to go through any questions make sense? I'm free [two time options].

Best,
[Your name]

synonyms: Let's set up a follow-up call

en.h1: “Let’s schedule another meeting” — what it might mean and how to reply
en.shortAnswer: A positive process signal: the investor is spending more time on you. It is still not a commitment. The strongest versions come with an agenda, a date, more senior attendees or specific data requests.

interpretations.possibility: Real progress in their evaluation process.
interpretations.contextualClues: A calendar invite arrives quickly; a more senior partner joins; they explain their process and timeline.

interpretations.possibility: Diligence on a specific concern they want resolved before going further.
interpretations.contextualClues: They name a topic (go-to-market, unit economics, technology) or request specific data in advance.

interpretations.possibility: Relationship-building without a near-term decision — some investors meet many times before deciding.
interpretations.contextualClues: Same person, no agenda, 'just catching up'; no mention of process or timing.

positiveSignals: A date and agenda are proposed quickly.
A more senior partner or specialist joins.
They request specific materials ahead of time.
They describe the next steps after this meeting.
weakSignals: The meeting keeps getting rescheduled.
No agenda and no new attendees.
Several meetings with no movement in their process.
en.clarifyingQuestion: Looking forward to it. What would be most useful for this conversation to resolve, and who else from your side will join?
en.recommendedAction: Confirm the meeting, ask what it should resolve, and prepare evidence for that topic. Ask about their process and timeline. Keep your other conversations moving at the same pace.
en.followUpTimingNote: Confirm within a day. Send any requested material before the meeting, and a short recap with next steps within 24 hours after it.
en.editableReplyTemplate:
Hi [Investor name],

Thanks — glad the conversation was useful. [Day/time] works well for us.

To make the most of the time: is there anything specific you'd like us to dig into — for example [topic, e.g. our sales pipeline or unit economics]? Happy to send material in advance.

And will anyone else from [Fund] be joining, so I can bring the right people from our side?

Best,
[Your name]

en.h1: “I’d like you to meet my partner” — what it might mean and how to reply
en.shortAnswer: Usually a positive process signal: your contact is willing to spend internal capital on you. It may be a champion building support, a required second opinion, or a specialist check. Prepare for fund-level questions, and ask your contact what the partner will care about.

interpretations.possibility: Your contact is acting as an internal champion and building support.
interpretations.contextualClues: The intro explains why they're excited; your contact stays involved and helps you prepare.

interpretations.possibility: A routine step — many funds require a second partner's view before going further.
interpretations.contextualClues: They describe it as standard process; no particular enthusiasm or concern is signalled.

interpretations.possibility: A specialist check on a concern — the partner has domain or technical expertise.
interpretations.contextualClues: The partner's background matches a risk discussed in your first meeting.

positiveSignals: The intro is framed with a purpose and a date.
Your original contact stays involved and offers preparation tips.
Material requests or process explanations follow.
weakSignals: The new partner seems unfamiliar with your company.
The intro arrives without context or a timeframe.
Your original contact goes quiet after the handoff.
en.clarifyingQuestion: Thanks for the introduction. What would be most helpful to cover with [Partner name], and what are the next steps in your process after that?
en.recommendedAction: Prepare for broader, fund-level questions — market size, how big the outcome could be, portfolio fit. Ask your contact which concerns to address. Send a short pre-read so the partner arrives informed.
en.followUpTimingNote: Respond within a day and offer times. Send a recap within 24 hours of the partner meeting, copying your original contact.
en.editableReplyTemplate:
Hi [Investor name],

Thank you — I'd be glad to meet [Partner name].

To prepare well: is there anything you'd suggest we focus on for [Partner name] — for example [topic, e.g. market size or technical risk]? I'm happy to send a short pre-read in advance.

And so I can plan around it, what would typically come after this conversation in your process?

Best,
[Your name]

en.phrase: We need to see more traction.
synonyms: Come back when you have more revenue

en.h1: “We need to see more traction” — what it might mean and how to reply
en.shortAnswer: A real evidence gap, a stage mismatch, or a general objection that sits on top of a different concern. Ask which metric matters and at roughly what level — then decide whether that milestone fits your own plan before chasing it.

interpretations.possibility: A specific evidence gap — demand, growth rate, retention or revenue quality.
interpretations.contextualClues: They name a metric or ask detailed questions about cohorts, pipeline or churn.

interpretations.possibility: A stage mismatch: the fund usually backs companies with more history.
interpretations.contextualClues: Their recent deals are later-stage; the comment is about thresholds rather than your trajectory.

interpretations.possibility: A general objection masking another concern (team, market, competition).
interpretations.contextualClues: The meeting focused on other topics; no metric is named; the comment comes at the very end.

positiveSignals: They name the metric and a rough threshold.
They ask to hear when you reach it.
They engage with your numbers in detail.
weakSignals: No metric or threshold mentioned.
Their questions focused on something else entirely.
They don't respond to a request for clarification.
en.clarifyingQuestion: Which metric matters most to you — revenue, growth rate, retention or something else — and roughly what level would make a conversation worthwhile?
en.recommendedAction: Record the metric and threshold if given. Decide whether it fits your own plan — don't chase an arbitrary number for one investor. Prioritise investors who back companies at your current stage, and send a short update if you hit the milestone.
en.followUpTimingNote: Ask the clarifying question within a few days. Reconnect when the milestone is reached, with the data — not before.
en.editableReplyTemplate:
Hi [Investor name],

Thanks for being direct — that's useful.

So I understand what would move the needle: which metric matters most to you at our stage — [option A, e.g. monthly revenue], [option B, e.g. retention], or something else — and roughly what level would make a future conversation worthwhile?

If it lines up with our plan, I'd be glad to send a short update when we get there.

Best,
[Your name]

en.h1: “Come back when you have a lead investor” — what it might mean and how to reply
en.shortAnswer: Conditional interest at best — and sometimes a polite no. Some investors genuinely only follow; others use it to wait for someone else's validation. Count it as conditional, never as committed, and ask what cheque size and conditions would apply.

interpretations.possibility: Genuine follower appetite — the fund rarely or never leads and relies on a lead to set terms.
interpretations.contextualClues: Their portfolio shows few or no leads; they mention a cheque size or ask about the terms you're targeting.

interpretations.possibility: Interest that depends on validation: they want someone else to do the diligence and set the price.
interpretations.contextualClues: They ask who else you're talking to; enthusiasm is real but nothing concrete is offered.

interpretations.possibility: A soft decline with no real commitment behind it.
interpretations.contextualClues: No amount, no conditions, no request to be informed when a lead commits.

positiveSignals: They state a cheque size and conditions.
They offer introductions to potential leads.
They ask to be informed as soon as a lead commits.
weakSignals: No amount mentioned.
Enthusiasm without any detail.
They don't respond when you share an update on lead conversations.
en.clarifyingQuestion: That's helpful, thank you. If we secure a lead on terms in the range we discussed, what cheque size would you consider — and are there conditions on who the lead is?
en.recommendedAction: Record this as conditional, not committed, and don't count it toward your round total. Focus effort on finding a lead. Ask for introductions to funds that do lead at your stage.
en.followUpTimingNote: Reply within a couple of days. Contact them again when a lead has committed or term-sheet talks are advanced.
en.editableReplyTemplate:
Hi [Investor name],

Thanks — that's clear and helpful.

So I can plan the round properly: if we secure a lead on terms around [target terms or range], what cheque size would you consider, and do you have any requirements for who the lead is?

If any funds come to mind that typically lead at our stage, an introduction would be hugely appreciated. I'll let you know as soon as a lead is in place.

Best,
[Your name]

en.h1: No response after two follow-ups — what investor silence might mean
en.shortAnswer: Silence is a behaviour, not a message, so read it cautiously. It can be bandwidth, a lost email, a stalled internal process — or low interest. After two unanswered follow-ups, send one brief close-the-loop note and redirect your energy to active conversations.

interpretations.possibility: Bandwidth, travel or a crowded inbox — your email simply hasn't been prioritised.
interpretations.contextualClues: Earlier engagement was strong; the silence is short; they've replied promptly before.

interpretations.possibility: An internal process has stalled and they don't have an answer yet.
interpretations.contextualClues: They mentioned partner discussions or an investment committee; the silence follows a promised decision date.

interpretations.possibility: Low interest, communicated by not replying.
interpretations.contextualClues: Engagement was limited from the start; no concrete next step was ever agreed; several weeks have passed.

positiveSignals: They had previously agreed a concrete next step or decision date.
They engaged in detail earlier (questions, material requests).
Someone else at the fund is still responsive.
weakSignals: No concrete next step was ever agreed.
Several weeks of silence despite short, useful updates.
They've seen your follow-ups (e.g. replied to others) but not to you.
en.clarifyingQuestion: Is this still something you'd like to explore, or should I take it off your plate for now? Either answer is completely fine.
en.recommendedAction: Send one short close-the-loop message with a real update and a simple yes/no question. Then move them to 'inactive' in your pipeline and reallocate your attention. Don't send more chasers.
en.followUpTimingNote: Wait until a promised date has passed by a few business days (or about a week after a meeting). After two unanswered follow-ups, one final note 1–2 weeks later — then stop.
en.editableReplyTemplate:
Hi [Investor name],

I know things get busy, so I'll keep this short.

A quick update: [one concrete piece of progress].

Is [Company] still something you'd like to explore this round, or should I take it off your plate for now? Either answer is completely fine — it just helps me plan.

Best,
[Your name]

exampleScenario.description: Hypothetical: a partner promised a decision “by Friday”, then went quiet for two weeks despite two polite follow-ups. A stalled internal process and low interest are both plausible. The founder sends one close-the-loop note with a new customer win and a yes/no question, then focuses on two investors who are actively engaged.
